title: Back to the Basics: 2026
headline: Here we go again...for real this time
searchDescription: An honest reflection on the 'gifted kid' trap, over-relying on AI tools, and why 18 months of 'learning' led to fake depth. The plan to go back to basics and build real understanding in machine learning—one algorithm at a time
excerpt: Here we go again...for real this time

content.text: I've started this post about five times now. Each time, I tried to make it sound polished—inspirational, even. But that felt dishonest, and honestly, dishonesty is what got me here in the first place. So let me just say it plainly.
I need to be honest with you, and with myself.

On paper, I look like I know what I'm doing. Master's in mathematics. ML internship where I built a recommendation system. Research experience with SVMs, PCA, data preprocessing techniques for image recognition, neural networks. Completed Andrew Ng's Machine Learning and Deep Learning specializations. Projects involving CNNs, NLP, the whole deal.
But here's the truth: I've been faking depth this whole time.

I finish courses but don't build anything after. I start projects but lean on AI tools to get through the hard parts. I buy books—Hands-On Machine Learning by Aurélien Géron, Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann, Deep Learning by Goodfellow—and I don't finish them. I've picked up that Hands-On ML book more times than I can count. It's still sitting there, half-read.

For over a year and a half, I've been spinning: Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Java, Go, Python, TypeScript, DevOps, LeetCode, System Design, Automation. Touching everything, mastering nothing. I keep telling myself, "it's part of the process...I'll figure it out as I go." As of the time you're reading this, nothing has been figured out. And I've grown so tired of it—tired of the cycle, tired of the excuses, and mostly, tired of knowing I'm capable of more but never proving it.
Which brings me to something I don't really talk about.
The "Gifted Kid" Trap

Growing up, academics came easy. A's were normal. I won a national math competition in college. Graduated one of the best students in my department. People called me smart—said they "wished they had my brain." Teachers expected great things. Family and friends still do.
Somewhere along the way, that became the problem.

When your identity is built on being "the smart one," failure feels like exposure. Like the whole thing was a lie. So you avoid situations where you might actually struggle. You start things but don't finish—because an incomplete project isn't a failed project, right? You buy books instead of reading them because owning knowledge feels safer than confronting what you don't know. You try to protect yourself from being exposed as some kind of fraud. Oh, so he wasn't all that smart after all...oh, so he too can fail. You become too scared of the voices that could be. So that's what I focused on: protecting that image instead of building real skill.
But the image doesn't build anything. It just keeps you stuck. And while I was busy protecting it, I developed another problem—one I'm almost embarrassed to admit.
The AI Tools Irony
Here's the part that keeps me up at night.

I want to become a Machine Learning Engineer. That's the goal. But I've been letting AI tools do my thinking for me. I've used them to debug code I should've struggled through. To write functions I should've written myself. To shortcut the exact friction that would've made me grow.

And the worst part? I got good at it. I learned how to prompt my way through problems—how to copy, paste, tweak, and move on without ever really understanding what I just implemented. The code worked. The projects got "finished." But when I'd come back weeks later, I couldn't explain my own work. Couldn't modify it without asking the AI again. I was building a portfolio of things I didn't actually understand.

The projects on my resume? I leaned on AI for a lot of them. Not completely—but enough that I know my understanding isn't as deep as it should be. Enough that if you sat me down and asked me to rebuild any of them from scratch, without assistance, I'd struggle. And that's the problem: I have the credentials without the confidence. The output without the understanding.

There's something almost funny about wanting to build AI systems while letting AI build my understanding for me. Except it's not funny. It's why I'm still here, eighteen months later, feeling like I'm running in place.
And I got a hard reminder of that last year.
The Failed Interview

In 2024, I interviewed with Google—one of my dream companies. I thought I'd ace it because, you know, smartass over here. Boy, was I wrong. With little preparation, I completely fumbled the last session. Honestly, I had never even seen a LeetCode problem like it. Everything went downhill after that. The callback was heartbreaking.

I told myself I'd improve. Grind harder. Come back stronger and hopefully get another shot the next year. But I didn't—not really. I picked up the same books, started the same tutorials, abandoned the same projects. The cycle just repeated. The year is ending, and I don't feel like I've accomplished what I set my mind to—including at least 100 deep ML problems and 250 LeetCode problems.
Cycles feel like motion. You're busy. You're "learning." But you're just walking in circles. The hardest part of learning isn't starting—it's admitting you've been doing it wrong.
So let me be clear about where I actually stand.
What I Actually Have

I'm not starting from zero. I have a math background most people breaking into ML don't have. I work as a Software QA Engineer now, which has taught me discipline: how to think systematically, how to catch what's broken, how to build reliable systems. I've done real ML work before—recommendation systems, predictive models, research with real datasets.
The foundation is there. What's missing is consistency. Depth. Finishing what I start. Doing the work myself, even when it's hard—especially when it's hard.

I think part of my problem has been treating learning like consumption instead of construction. Watching lectures, reading articles, skimming documentation—and calling it progress. But information isn't understanding. You don't actually know something until you've built with it, broken it, debugged it, and explained it to someone else. That's the gap I need to close.
And closing it starts with a different approach entirely.
The Plan for 2026

This year, I'm going back to basics—not because I'm a beginner, but because I want to actually own what I know. I want to understand how and why things work. I want to read documentation, struggle, fail, learn, try, and keep trying. I want to break out of my shell, put myself out there, contribute to meaningful work, and receive meaningful feedback.
Here's what that looks like in practice:

items: Code algorithms from scratch: No importing sklearn and calling it a day. I'm writing linear regression, logistic regression, decision trees, SVMs—from the math up. I want to derive the gradients by hand, implement the optimization loops myself, and understand what every line of code is doing. If I can't build it from a blank file, I don't understand it. The goal isn't just to make things work—it's to know why they work.

Learn in public: Every concept I learn, I write about. This space becomes my accountability system. If I can't explain something clearly, I don't know it well enough. Writing forces precision—it exposes gaps in your thinking that reading alone never reveals. You reading this? You're part of the mechanism now. Sorry not sorry.

Limit the AI crutch: I'm not saying I'll never use AI tools—that's unrealistic in 2026. But I'm setting boundaries. First attempt is always manual. I sit with the problem, struggle with it, Google it the old-fashioned way, read the docs, try different approaches. Only after I've genuinely tried do I use AI to check my thinking or get unstuck. The learning happens in the struggle, and I've been skipping that part for too long.

Kaggle competitions: Real data, real problems, real deadlines. I'm committing to at least one competition per quarter. The goal isn't to win—it's to get uncomfortable and build under pressure. To work with messy datasets that don't come pre-cleaned. To see how my skills hold up when there's no tutorial guiding me.

Replicate papers: By the end of 2026, I want to read ML papers and implement them. Not summarize—implement. Actually build the architecture, train it, and reproduce the results (or understand why I couldn't). I'm starting with foundational papers—LeNet, AlexNet, maybe the original transformer—before moving to more recent work. That's the bar.

Finish the books: I'm picking two: Hands-On Machine Learning and Designing Machine Learning Systems. No new books until these are done. No more collecting—just completing. I'll go chapter by chapter, do every exercise, build every project. If it takes all year, it takes all year.

Show everything: No more private or public half-finished repos. Wins, failures, confusion, breakthroughs—all of it gets documented and shared. I want a trail of evidence I can point to. Not for anyone else, really. For myself. Proof that I actually did the work.

content.text: But none of this matters if I don't change how I approach learning itself. So before I dive into any of this, there are a few structural changes I'm making.
How I'm Restructuring

items: Time-boxing over perfection: I used to wait until I "felt ready" to build something. Spoiler: that feeling never came. I'd research endlessly, watch one more tutorial, read one more article—all to avoid the discomfort of starting before I felt prepared. Now I'm setting hard deadlines. Learning decision trees? Three days for theory, two days to implement. Done is the goal. I can refactor later. Finished beats perfect, and imperfect action beats perfect paralysis every single time.

Active recall over passive consumption: Reading a chapter means nothing if I can't explain it the next day without looking. I'm done highlighting passages and pretending that's learning. Every study session now ends with me closing the book and writing down what I learned—from memory. If I can't recall it, I didn't learn it. Flashcards, practice problems, teaching concepts out loud like I'm explaining to someone else. The discomfort of forgetting is the point. That's where learning actually happens.

One thing at a time: No more learning five languages and three frameworks simultaneously. That scattered approach is exactly how I ended up here - knowing a little about everything, not enough about anything. Depth over breadth. ML fundamentals first. Everything else waits.

Weekly reviews: Every Sunday, I sit down for an honest audit. The questions: What did I actually build this week? What can I explain now that I couldn't before? Where did I get stuck—and did I push through or give up? What's the one thing I'm carrying into next week? I'm keeping a simple log, nothing fancy—just a running document. If too many weeks pass with weak answers, that's a signal. No more lying to myself about "being busy." Either I made real progress, or I didn't.

content.text: These aren't revolutionary ideas. But doing them consistently? That would be new for me.
An Invitation
I don't know if everything I post will make sense to you. Some of it will be technical breakdowns. Some will be me working through concepts in real time. Some might be messy.

But if you're an engineer who feels stuck—if you've been "learning" for months without real progress, if you're a beginner looking for explanations that don't assume you already know everything—stick around.
Honestly, I'm not sure where this goes. But I know I'm done spinning.
2026 is the year I go back to basics and actually finish what I start.

Now I want to hear from you. Have you been stuck in a similar loop? Are you starting fresh this year too? Drop a comment, share your story, or just say hi. And if this resonated with you, share it with someone who might need to read it. Sometimes knowing you're not alone in the struggle is enough to take the first step.
See you next week.
Prince Agyei Tuffour
